idiom_name: hand-written per-type combine functions with out-params and an accumulated error list
implementation_notes: C has no generics, no type classes and no higher-kinded types, so pure/ap cannot be expressed once for all contexts: each payload type gets its own combining function that calls every independent producer, then merges the success values and the failures. What replaces the classic structure is that convention - a tagged result struct (returned by value, C99 designated initializers) carrying a value or a list of error codes, plus one combine function per type. The classic applicative form is still justified when independent parses must all be reported (config loading, protocol field decoding): the alternative, checking each call with if-errno-return, is fail-fast and loses every error after the first.
pitfalls: Both producers must be called before the failure test: short-circuiting the second call (the natural C reflex) silently discards its errors and turns the code back into fail-fast behaviour.
The merged error list needs an owner: returning a pointer to an error buffer that lives in a producer's stack frame is a dangling write; let the combine function own the destination buffer.
There is no generic lift2: a macro-based 'generic' combine loses the type checking that the per-type struct was buying, and a void* payload reintroduces casts at every call site.
Error codes accumulate and must be stable across translation units; an enum per module plus an explicit mapping keeps the accumulated list meaningful to callers.
